question: Which statement best describes What SSR actually does?
options: The simplest way to force SSR for a route is to make its data fetch uncacheable. A fetch with cache: 'no-store' is re-run on every request, which opts the whole route into dynamic (server-per-request) rendering. Use this when the data genuinely changes between requests.

On each incoming request the server runs your Server Component, fetches data, renders React to HTML, and streams it to the browser. The user sees real content immediately and crawlers index it, but the server does work for every single request. In the App Router this happens automatically whenever a route reads request-specific data.

Reading request-only data — cookies(), headers(), draftMode(), or the searchParams prop — depends on the incoming request, so Next.js cannot pre-render the page at build time and automatically switches it to SSR. This is how personalized pages (per-user content based on a session cookie) become dynamic.

You can opt an entire route segment into SSR explicitly with a route segment config export, regardless of how its fetches are cached. This is useful when you want a guarantee that the route is always dynamic, or to document the intent for reviewers.

question: Which statement best describes force-dynamic route config?
options: SSG renders once at build and serves frozen HTML from a CDN — fastest and cheapest but stale until rebuild. SSR renders fresh per request — always current but slower and costlier. Choose SSR only when content must reflect the current request (per-user, per-moment); otherwise prefer SSG or ISR.
